description: Our app lets roommates split rent and utilities. Everyone pays their share into a group balance we hold, and we pay the landlord and utility companies from it on the due date.
Students can send money to each other for textbooks, concert tickets, or splitting food. Balances stay in the app until they cash out to their bank.
Users buy Bitcoin and Ethereum with a debit card, and we keep the coins in wallets we control. They can send coins to friends or sell back to dollars and withdraw.
Send money abroad from the US to the Philippines and Vietnam. Users pay by bank transfer, we convert to pesos or dong, and recipients get a deposit to their bank or e wallet.
We sell prepaid Visa gift cards online. Buyers load any amount, and the recipient can spend it at any store that takes Visa.

A bill pay app where you link your bank and pay any company you owe, like your phone bill or car loan. We pull the money from your account and send the payment ourselves. We don't have deals with the billers.
We build online store software for small businesses. Checkout payments go straight to the seller's own payment processor account; we just charge a monthly subscription.
A national bank adding a feature that lets account holders send money to anyone with a phone number.
Budgeting app that connects to your bank accounts to track spending and set savings goals. We can see balances but cannot move any money.
Online food ordering for restaurants. Each restaurant contracts with us to accept payments on its behalf, and the customer's order is considered paid to the restaurant when we receive the money.
Subscription billing software. We schedule and retry charges for gyms and streaming services, but all payments settle directly into each business's own merchant account.
Expense tracking app for small businesses. It scans receipts and syncs everything with their accounting software. We don't move any money.

Online marketplace for handmade goods. Buyers pay at checkout and sellers get paid once the item ships. Our payment processor handles the money, but we're not sure if it sits in our account or theirs.
Freelance marketplace for designers. Clients fund a project up front, and we release payment to the freelancer when the client approves the work.
Buy now, pay later at checkout. We pay the merchant in full immediately, and the shopper pays us back in four installments.
Crowdfunding site for personal causes like medical bills and school costs. Donors give through our site and we send the money to the campaign organizer.
Payroll for small businesses. We pull the payroll total from the employer's account into ours, then pay each employee by direct deposit.
Event ticketing platform. Fans buy tickets through us, and we pay the event organizer after the show, minus our fees.

We help immigrants in the US send money home. You pay in our app with a bank account or debit card, and we deliver the cash to your family's bank account, mobile wallet or a pickup spot in over 100 countries. We charge a small fee and make money on the exchange rate.

We are a data connector for other apps. When a user links their bank, we pass the app their account balance and transaction history so it can build a budget or check their income. We never hold money and we have no way to start a payment.

Online marketplace for handmade jewelry. Buyers check out on our site, sellers ship the order, and sellers get their earnings in their bank account a few days later. The payments run in the background and we set the payout schedule.

Hold and send money in 40 currencies. A freelancer in the US can fund an account from their bank, convert to euros at the real exchange rate, and send it to any European bank account. Customers can also keep a balance in our app.
We are a bank with branches in 14 states. Customers open checking accounts, deposit paychecks, and send wires or Zelle payments to other people from our mobile app.

Payroll made simple for small businesses. The owner types in hours, we calculate taxes, and employees get paid by direct deposit on payday. Owners fund payroll with us a couple of days early, and we use a bank partner for the transfers.
Pay your friends with a few taps. Split dinner, send rent to your roommate, or chip in for a gift. The money sits in your balance in our app until you send it on or move it to your bank.
We design and sell a small hardware device that stores your crypto private keys offline. You alone control your keys. We cannot see your coins or move them, and we never process transfers.

Decentralized token swap site. Users connect their own wallet and trade tokens through open-source smart contracts. We built the website, and we keep a small fee from each swap that goes to a wallet we own. We do not hold user keys.

Pay any bill with a credit card, even if the landlord or school doesn't take cards. You charge the amount to your card on our site, and we send your landlord a check or bank transfer. We charge about 3%.
Accounting software for small shops. It tracks sales and expenses, creates reports for tax time, and matches entries with your bank transactions. Customers pay a monthly subscription for it.

A freelancing site for designers and writers. Clients start a project and put the milestone payment into escrow on our platform. When the client approves the work, the freelancer is paid. We keep a 10% cut.

A simple place to buy, hold and send crypto. Customers link a bank account, buy Bitcoin and USDC, and we keep it safe in our wallets for them. They can send it to any other wallet or cash it out to a bank account whenever they want.
Our coffee shop app lets customers load a balance on their account and pay at the counter. The balance can only be used at our stores, and it cannot be transferred or withdrawn as cash.

A creator game platform. Players buy our virtual currency with real money and spend it on items in games made by other users. Creators who earn enough can exchange the currency for real dollars, paid out to their bank account.

Get paid by customers abroad. Companies around the world pay freelancers and sellers into a virtual account with us. We hold the money in the freelancer's balance, and then they withdraw it to their local bank.

An app for friends and flatmates to keep track of who owes who. You add shared expenses, and the app shows who should pay whom. When someone pays back, they mark it as settled. The app does not process the payments itself.
We are the city's official online utility bill payment page. Residents pay water and trash bills by card, and under our contract with the city, paying us is the same as paying the city.

Our delivery startup in Houston lets drivers send up to $300 of their weekly pay to a family member's bank account in Mexico. We receive the driver's payout in our account, convert it to pesos, and deposit it through a partner bank in Mexico.

We make invoicing software for freelance designers: invoices, reminders, and an unpaid-invoice tracker for $12 a month. Clients pay the designer through their own bank transfer or the designer's own card processor account, and the money goes straight to the designer.

Friend groups of 4-10 put $50-$500 each into a shared trip wallet in our app. We hold the pooled balance in an account at our sponsor bank, and the organizer taps to send exact amounts to the hotel, the Airbnb host, or whichever friend fronted a cost.

Fans tip streamers $1-$100 on our site by card. We pay each streamer once their balance reaches $50, minus 10%. Our terms call us the streamer's payment agent, but a lawyer hasn't reviewed whether that wording is enough in every state.

We operate 40 Bitcoin ATMs in Texas gas stations. A customer feeds in up to $2,000 in cash, scans any wallet QR code, and we buy the coins and send them to that wallet, which is usually someone else's.

The City of Plano signed a contract naming our parking app its official collection agent. Drivers pay by card in the app, and the money settles each night directly into the city's own bank account. We get a flat fee per transaction from the city.

Parents in India pay their kid's tuition at US universities through our portal. They pay us in rupees, we convert, and we send dollars to the school. We're negotiating contracts that may name us each university's agent, but none are signed yet.

Our API is used by a staffing marketplace. The marketplace's clients fund our pooled FBO account by ACH debit on Monday, and on Wednesday we credit each contractor's bank account for their invoice amount after verifying their identity.

Tablet POS app for food trucks, $39 a month. Card payments run through each truck owner's own processor account with their own merchant ID, and deposits go to the owner's bank. We never receive any sales money.

Employees can take up to 40% of their earned but unpaid wages early through our app, and we front the cash from our own funds. The employer repays us out of the next payroll file. Counsel hasn't decided if that is a loan or a transfer of the employer's money.
Our laundromat chain in Ohio sells money orders at the counter for a $1 fee, up to $500 each. Customers use them to pay rent and bills.
Read-only analytics dashboard for DeFi wallets. Users paste a public wallet address to see profit and loss history, and we hold no keys, can't sign transactions, and never touch user funds.

Amateur esports tournaments run by us. Players pay a $10 entry fee on our site, and the top 3 get prize money from the pool within 48 hours. We aren't sure whether the pooled fees count as our own revenue or as player funds we're transmitting.
We help small Texas importers pay overseas suppliers. They wire us dollars, we convert, and we send Vietnamese dong to the supplier's bank in Ho Chi Minh City, usually $5,000-$50,000 per transfer.
Coffee chain loyalty card. Customers load $5-$100 into the app and spend it only at our own stores. The balance can't be sent to other people or cashed out.

Pay-later checkout button for online stores. We pay the merchant up front and collect four biweekly payments from the shopper. We also pass the shopper's refund back to the merchant's account when an order is returned.
Unbanked customers in New York pay cash at our storefronts, and we pay their electric, phone and water bills for them from our own bank account the same day. We charge $3 per bill.

We sell loan origination software to credit unions. The credit union's staff review applications in our dashboard and fund approved loans from the credit union's own accounts. Our fee is a yearly license.

Donors pick up to 20 charities and pay once by card. We keep the donations in a pooled account at our bank and send each charity its share on the 1st of the month. Two advisers told us we need registration, a third said no.

Our title company software holds buyers' earnest money in a trust account at a partner bank for up to 3 days before releasing it to the seller. We can't tell whether escrow rules in Florida cover us or whether we still need a license.

Sendly is a Chicago-based app for sending money to friends and family across the US who don't use the same app, a common problem when a relative only has a bank account. The sender pays by debit card or ACH, and we hold the funds in our own settlement account until we send an ACH credit to the recipient's bank the next business day. Recipients enter their bank details through a text-message link and don't need an account with us. We charge senders a flat $1.99 fee per transfer.

PawPath is a Denver-based marketplace where pet owners book vetted dog walkers, and owners are often wary of prepaying strangers. Owners pay through our app at booking, and we hold the funds in our own bank account for seven days to cover disputes. We then pay each walker by ACH direct deposit and keep a 15% platform fee. Walkers are independent contractors and never receive money directly from the owner.

Our Seattle-based studio's mobile card game lets US players load real dollars into an in-app wallet using a card or Apple Pay. Players can send any part of their balance to any other player, so they can buy and sell in-game items for cash. They can also cash out to a bank account or PayPal at any time for a $0.50 fee. Balances are in US dollars, never expire, and are held in an account we control.

RentFlex, based in Atlanta, helps US tenants whose landlords accept only checks or ACH pay rent by credit card, for rewards or cash-flow reasons. We charge the tenant's card plus a 2.9% convenience fee, then send the rent to the landlord by ACH or a mailed check from our own account. We typically hold the funds for two to three business days before sending. The landlord has no contract with us and never has to onboard.

We are a Miami-based company running a custodial stablecoin service for US users who want to move dollars quickly without a bank. Users deposit USDC to wallets we control and record on our books, and can transfer any amount to another user by entering an email address. The recipient can keep the balance with us or withdraw it to a linked US bank account or an external wallet. We charge a 0.5% fee on withdrawals.

Our Austin-based payout API is built for US businesses that pay many freelancers and want a single integration. Clients wire money into pooled accounts titled in our name, and we credit it to each client's ledger balance. When a client submits a payment instruction, we send an ACH credit from the pooled account to the freelancer's US bank account. Freelancers have no relationship with us other than as payees.

Settle is a New York-based social payments app that lets friends keep a balance and split costs like dinners and utilities. User balances are held in an FBO account at our partner bank, and our own ledger tracks each user's share. Users can add funds by debit card, send to other users instantly, or withdraw to an external debit card. We charge 1.5% on instant withdrawals.

We are a Portland-based company building booking and client-management software for independent US hair salons that used to take payments by phone. Each salon connects its own Stripe account, so card payments settle directly from Stripe to the salon's bank account. We are not a party to the payments, never touch client funds, and are not the merchant of record. We charge salons a flat $79 monthly subscription.

We are an FDIC-insured, Ohio-chartered community bank with 14 branches across Ohio serving households and small businesses. Customers can initiate ACH and wire transfers from their own checking accounts through our online and mobile banking platform. Every transfer is made from a deposit account held at the bank itself. We are examined by our state banking regulator and the FDIC.

We operate the online bill-pay portal for three municipal water utilities in Georgia that lack their own payment systems. Residents pay on our site by card or ACH, and under our written contract with each utility, payment to us counts as payment to the utility, so the resident's obligation is discharged at that moment. We remit collected funds to each utility's bank account the next business day. The utility, not the resident, pays us a flat per-transaction fee.

We sell tickets for 22 independent theatres across the Midwest that don't have their own online box office. Each venue appoints us as its sales agent under a signed agency agreement, and the venue is deemed paid when a customer completes checkout. We settle collected sales to each theatre weekly, less our 6% commission. Customers pay us only for tickets and have no other relationship with us.

Harbor is a San Francisco-based self-custody crypto wallet app for US users who want full control of their own assets. Private keys are generated and stored only on the user's device, and we have no access to funds and no ability to move or freeze them. Users sign transactions locally, and our servers only relay the signed transaction to the public network. We earn revenue from a monthly subscription for premium features like portfolio analytics.

We are a Nashville company selling payroll software to small US restaurants that otherwise run payroll by hand. Owners calculate wages, taxes, and tips in our app, then export a NACHA payment file and upload it to their own bank. Employee pay moves directly from the employer's bank account to each employee's bank account. We never receive or hold funds, and we charge a $40 monthly subscription.

I teach guitar from Nashville, Tennessee, and sell my own video courses to students across the US through my own website. Students pay by card through a standard checkout, and the money lands in my own business bank account. I am both the seller and the party who gets paid. No other party receives funds from the transaction.

Wickline is a Vermont-based marketplace for handmade candles made by US sellers where buyers check out on our site and sellers are paid after the item ships. Card processing runs through a third-party payments provider, and seller accounts are set up using Stripe Connect. Sellers set their own prices and ship directly to buyers, and we take a 10% commission. Our final contract with the provider is still being negotiated.

Our Boston-based app splits rent and utilities for roommates in shared apartments across the US. One roommate is designated as the payer to the landlord, and the others send their share to that person through our app, usually the same day. Transfers run through a payment processor we integrate with, and we charge a small monthly fee per household. The landlord is paid by the designated roommate, not by us.

TipJar is a Los Angeles-based tipping platform for US streamers and podcasters. Fans tip by card, and creators receive a payout once a month after reaching a $25 balance. Charges run through our payments processor, and each creator can see an accumulated balance in our dashboard. We take a 5% platform fee on each tip.

We are a Minneapolis-based startup offering a prepaid allowance card for US kids ages 8 to 17. Parents load money onto the card from their bank account, children spend it in stores and online, and parents can move unused funds between their children's cards in the app. The cards are issued by a bank partner through a program manager, and we operate the app. Parents can also set merchant-category limits.

Our Brooklyn-based crypto on-ramp lets US users buy tokens with a US-issued debit card on partner websites. A partner exchange executes the purchase, and we deliver the tokens to the user's own wallet address. In some flows the card payment settles into our bank account for a few minutes before we forward it to the exchange. In other flows the exchange charges the card itself and we only supply the interface.

We are a Phoenix-based group travel app where a trip organizer collects each friend's share inside the app and then books the hotel. Funds are pooled in an account at our bank partner until the booking is confirmed, and refunded to the friends if the booking fails. The account is titled in our name for the benefit of the group. The final partner agreement is still being negotiated, so it is undecided whether the bank or we will be the party of record.
